blocks.p: When they had left the Shepherds, they soon came to the place where Christian had met Turn-away, who lived in the town of Apostasy. Here Mr. Great-heart, their guide, reminded them of him.

“This is the place where Christian met Turn-away,” he said, “the man who carried the record of his rebellion on his back. And I can tell you this about him: he would listen to no counsel, and once he had fallen, no persuasion could stop him. When he came to the place of the Cross and the Tomb, he met someone who told him to look there; but he gnashed his teeth and stamped his foot, and said he was resolved to go back to his own town. Before he reached the gate he met Evangelist, who offered to lay hands on him and turn him back into the way. But Turn-away resisted him, and after treating him with great contempt, he climbed over the wall and so escaped his hands.” [Heb. 10:26-29]
Then they went on; and just at the place where Little-Faith had been robbed long before, there stood a man with his sword drawn and his face all bloody.
“Who are you?” said Mr. Great-heart.

“I am a man named Valiant-for-truth,” he answered. “I am a pilgrim, and I am going to the Celestial City. As I was on my way, three men set upon me and put three things to me: first, whether I would become one of them; second, whether I would go back where I came from; or third, whether I would die on the spot. To the first I answered that I had been an honest man for a long time, so they could hardly expect me to throw in my lot with thieves now. [Prov. 1:10-14] Then they demanded what I had to say to the second. I told them that if I had found no trouble in the place I came from, I would never have left it at all; but finding it altogether unsuitable for me, and very unprofitable, I left it for this road. Then they asked what I said to the third. I told them that my life had cost far too much for me to give it away lightly. ‘Besides,’ I said, ‘you have no business putting choices like these to me; so if you lay a hand on me, it is at your own peril.’ Then these three, Wild-head, Inconsiderate, and Pragmatic, drew their swords on me, and I drew mine on them.

“So we fell to it, one against three, for more than three hours. They have left on me, as you see, some marks of their valor, and they have carried away some of mine. They are only just gone. I suppose they heard your horses coming, as the saying goes, and took to their heels.”
“But those were great odds,” said Mr. Great-heart. “Three against one.”

“True; but few or many are nothing to the man who has the truth on his side. ‘Though an army should encamp against me,’ said one, ‘my heart shall not fear; though war should rise against me, in this I will be confident.’ [Ps. 27:3] Besides, I have read in the records that one man has fought a whole army. And how many did Samson kill with the jawbone of a donkey?” [Judg. 15:15-16]
“Why didn’t you cry out, so that someone might have come to your aid?”
“So I did, to my King, who I knew could hear me and send invisible help; and that was enough for me.”
“You have carried yourself well,” said Great-heart to Mr. Valiant-for-truth. “Let me see your sword.”
So he showed it to him. Great-heart took it in his hand and looked at it a while, and then he said, “Ha! It is a true Jerusalem blade.” [Isa. 2:3]

“It is. Give a man one of these blades, with a hand to wield it and the skill to use it, and he may take on an angel. He need not fear its failing him, if he only knows how to lay on. Its edges never dull. It will cut flesh and bone, soul and spirit, and all.” [Eph. 6:12-17; Heb. 4:12]
“But you fought a long time. I wonder you were not worn out.”

“I fought until my sword stuck to my hand; and when they were joined together, as if the sword grew out of my arm, and the blood ran down through my fingers, then I fought with the most courage of all.” [2 Sam. 23:10]
“You have done well. You have ‘resisted to the point of blood, striving against sin.’ You shall stay with us, and come in and go out with us, for we are your companions.”

Then they took him and washed his wounds, and gave him some of what they had to refresh him; and so they went on together. Now as they went, Mr. Great-heart questioned him about many things, because he delighted in him (for he dearly loved a man he found to be good with his hands), and because there were some in his company who were feeble and weak. First he asked what country he came from.
“I am from Dark-land,” said Valiant. “I was born there, and my father and mother are there still.”
“Dark-land,” said the guide. “Doesn’t that lie along the same coast as the City of Destruction?”

“Yes, it does. And this is what brought me on pilgrimage. A man named Mr. Tell-true came into our parts, and he told everyone what Christian had done, the man who went from the City of Destruction: how he had left his wife and children and taken up a pilgrim’s life. It was also reported, on good authority, how he had killed a serpent that came out to oppose him on his journey, and how he got through to where he meant to go. It was told, too, what a welcome he had at every one of his Lord’s lodgings, and above all when he came to the gates of the Celestial City; for there, the man said, he was received with the sound of trumpets by a company of Shining Ones. He told how all the bells in the city rang for joy at his arrival, and what golden garments he was dressed in, and many other things that I will not go into now. In a word, that man told the story of Christian and his travels in such a way that my heart was set burning to go after him; and neither father nor mother could hold me back. So I got away from them, and I have come this far on my way.”
“You came in at the gate, didn’t you?”
“Yes, yes; for the same man told us that it would all be for nothing if we did not begin by entering this way at the gate.”
“Look here,” said the guide to Christiana, “the pilgrimage of your husband, and what he gained by it, is spread abroad far and near.”
“Why,” said Valiant, “is this Christian’s wife?”
“Yes, it is; and these are her four sons.”
“What! And going on pilgrimage too?”
“Yes, indeed. They are following after him.”
“That gladdens my heart. Good man! How joyful he will be when he sees the ones who would not go with him enter after him through the gates into the City!”
“Without doubt it will be a comfort to him; for next to the joy of seeing himself there, it will be a joy to meet his wife and children there.”
“But now that you are on that subject, let me hear your opinion. Some people make a question of whether we shall know one another when we are there.”

“Do they think they will know themselves there, or rejoice to see themselves in that bliss? And if they think they will know themselves and rejoice, why not know others, and rejoice in their welfare too? Besides, our relations are our second selves. Though that state will be dissolved there, isn’t it reasonable to conclude that we shall be gladder to see them there than to find them missing?”
“Well, I see where you stand on this. Have you anything more to ask me about how I came to go on pilgrimage?”
“Yes. Were your father and mother willing for you to become a pilgrim?”
“Oh, no! They used every means imaginable to persuade me to stay at home.”
“What could they say against it?”
“They said it was an idle life; and that if I were not inclined to sloth and laziness myself, I would never think well of a pilgrim’s condition.”
“And what else did they say?”
“Why, they told me it was a dangerous way. ‘The most dangerous way in the world,’ they said, ‘is the way the pilgrims go.’”
“Did they show how this way is so dangerous?”
“Yes, in many particulars.”
“Name some of them.”

“They told me of the Swamp of Despair, where Christian was nearly smothered. They told me there were archers standing ready in Beelzebub Castle to shoot anyone who knocked at the Wicket Gate for entrance. They told me of the woods and the dark mountains; of the Hill Difficulty; of the lions; and of the three giants, Bloody-man, Maul, and Slay-good. They said, moreover, that a foul fiend haunted the Valley of Humiliation, and that Christian was almost robbed of his life by him. ‘Besides,’ they said, ‘you must go through the Valley of the Shadow of Death, where the hobgoblins are; where the light is darkness; where the way is full of snares, pits, traps, and nets.’ They told me also of Giant Despair, and of Doubting Castle, and of the ruin that pilgrims had met with there. Then they said I must cross the Enchanted Ground, which was dangerous. And after all that, I would come to a river with no bridge over it, and that river lay between me and the Celestial Country.”
“And was that all?”
“No. They also told me that this way was full of deceivers, and of people who lay in wait to turn good men out of the path.”
“How did they make that out?”

“They told me that Mr. Worldly Wiseman lay in wait there to deceive. They said that Formalist and Hypocrisy were constantly on the road. They said that Mr. Self-Interest, or Talkative, or Demas would be sure to pick me up; that the Flatterer would catch me in his net; or that, like green-headed Ignorance, I would presume to go on to the gate, only to be sent back, as he always was, to the hole in the side of the hill, and made to take the back way to hell.”
“I grant you that was enough to discourage anyone. But did they stop there?”

“No, wait. They also told me of many who had tried that way in the old days, and gone a long way along it, to see if they could find something of the glory that so many had talked about for so long; and how they came back again and made fools of themselves, in front of the whole country, for ever setting a foot out of doors on that path. And they named several who had done so: Obstinate and Pliable, Mistrust and Timid, Turn-away and old Atheist, and more besides, some of whom, they said, had gone far to see what they could find, and not one of them had found enough advantage in going to weigh a feather.”
“Did they say anything more to discourage you?”

“Yes. They told me of one Mr. Fearing, who was a pilgrim, and how he found this way so lonely that he never had a comfortable hour on it. Also that Mr. Despondency had nearly starved on it. And, something I had almost forgotten, that Christian himself, about whom there had been such a noise, after all his ventures for a heavenly crown, had certainly drowned in the Black River and never gone a foot farther, however it had been hushed up.”
“And did none of these things discourage you?”
“No. They seemed like so many nothings to me.”
“How did that come about?”
“Why, I still believed what Mr. Tell-true had said, and that carried me past them all.”
“Then this was your victory: your faith.”
“It was. I believed, by the grace of God, and so I came out, got onto the way, fought everyone who set themselves against me, and, by believing, have come to this place.”
